property_summary: After any successful Put(...) call by an address, the caller's stored Acc[msg.sender].balance increases by exactly the sent msg.value (i.e., Put always credits the sender with the deposited amount); the mutated modifier that never resets the lock can cause later Put calls to behave differently (fail/revert) for the same sender, breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and deposit amount, calling Put increments that caller's stored Acc[caller].balance by the deposited msg.value (i.e., Put succeeds and credits the sender); the mutant that never clears the reentrancy lock can cause subsequent Put calls from the same caller to revert/fail, breaking this universal success-and-credit property for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero deposit amount, the reference contract allows the caller to successfully call Put and increases address(c).balance by that amount on each independent call; the mutant that never clears the reentrancy lock can cause a subsequent Put to revert (or fail) for the same caller leading to a mismatch in address(c).balance for some fuzzed inputs.

For any depositor address and deposit amount, if the depositor's first Put call succeeds (credits balance and increases contract balance), then a second Put call from the same depositor with the same amount will also succeed (i.e., Put does not permanently lock out the caller); the mutant that never clears the reentrancy lock can cause the second Put to fail for some inputs.

For any depositor and deposit amount (>=1 wei) the reference contract always allows a subsequent Put call from the same depositor to succeed (i.e., the call does not permanently revert); the mutant that never resets the reentrancy lock can make a later Put revert for the same depositor, violating this liveness property.

After any Put(...) call by any sender with any value, the contract's stored unlockTime for that sender is never in the past (i.e. unlockTime >= block.timestamp) — the reference enforces this by taking max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp), while the mutant that assigns unlockTime = _unlockTime can set a past timestamp and violate this.

After any Put called by an address with any value and _unlockTime, the reference guarantees Acc[addr].unlockTime >= block.timestamp (it clamps to now), whereas the mutant that assigns unlockTime = _unlockTime can set it < block.timestamp and thus violate this invariant.

For any caller and any Put call with msg.value > 0, the reference C guarantees that after Put completes the stored Acc[caller].balance increased by msg.value while the mutant may set unlockTime arbitrarily; we assert the balance invariant (balance increases by exactly the sent amount) which holds in the reference but the mutant breaks for some inputs only when reentrancy during LogFile.AddMessage or other external behavior can reorder state — to force difference, we deploy an attacker Log contract whose AddMessage reenters and causes the mutant to mis-update balance while the reference remains correct.

For any caller, after Put(...) returns the contract's stored Acc[caller].unlockTime is never less than the pre-call block.timestamp (the reference clamps to now), whereas the mutant that assigns unlockTime = _unlockTime can set it in the past and thus violate this invariant for some fuzzed _unlockTime values.

For any caller and any Put(_unlockTime, msg.value), the reference ensures that after Put returns Acc[caller].balance increased by exactly msg.value (balance_before + msg.value == balance_after); the mutant can be forced to violate this by deploying a malicious Log contract whose AddMessage re-enters and disturbs state ordering causing the observed final balance to be incorrect.

For any caller and any provided _unlockTime, after calling Put(...) the contract's recorded Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime equals max(_unlockTime, block.timestamp) (the reference preserves the caller's requested future unlock time; the mutant always sets it to block.timestamp, breaking this rule for inputs where _unlockTime > block.timestamp).

For any caller and any provided _unlockTime, after Put the stored Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime is >= block.timestamp and equals _unlockTime when _unlockTime > block.timestamp (i.e., the contract preserves a future unlockTime); the mutant that forces unlockTime = block.timestamp breaks this for inputs where _unlockTime > block.timestamp.

For any caller and any provided _unlockTime, after calling Put the stored Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime is at least the provided _unlockTime whenever the provided _unlockTime is in the future (>= block.timestamp); the mutant that forces unlockTime = block.timestamp can violate this when _unlockTime > block.timestamp.

For any caller and any provided _unlockTime, after calling Put the stored Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime is either equal to block.timestamp or equal to the provided _unlockTime; the mutant that always sets unlockTime = block.timestamp can violate this when the caller supplies a future _unlockTime (i.e., when _unlockTime > block.timestamp) — we express this as: if _unlockTime != block.timestamp then Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime == _unlockTime (so the reference preserves non-now requested times), which the mutant breaks for some fuzzed _unlockTime.

For any caller and any provided _unlockTime, after Put is called the stored Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime is either equal to block.timestamp or greater than block.timestamp exactly when the caller supplied a future time (i.e., Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime >= min(_unlockTime, block.timestamp)); the mutant that always sets unlockTime = block.timestamp violates this for some future _unlockTime by making it equal to block.timestamp instead of preserving the future value.

After any caller invokes Put with some payable amount, the contract's stored Acc[caller].balance increases by exactly the sent msg.value; the mutant that omits updating balance can be detected because for some inputs Acc[caller].balance will NOT reflect the sent value.

For any caller and any nonzero payable amount, after calling Put(...) the caller's recorded Acc[caller].balance is at least the amount they just sent (reference increments balance; mutant omits increment so this can fail).

For any caller, if they call Put(...) sending a positive ether amount and their previous stored balance is less than MinSum, then after Put their recorded Acc[caller].balance equals the sent amount (reference updates balance from zero; mutant that omits the increment leaves balance unchanged and thus violates this).

For any caller and any nonzero payable value sent to Put, the reference contract records that caller as having a nonzero Acc[msg.sender].unlockTime at or after the call time and also records a log entry (LogFile.History length increases) reflecting the Put; the mutant still sets unlockTime and logs but fails to increase Acc[msg.sender].balance—so we instead assert that when a caller later is able to Collect that amount (i.e., Collect succeeds for that caller withdrawing up to their recorded balance), then the contract's recorded balance must be at least the total ETH the caller has ever sent via Put; the mutant will permit a Collect to succeed while recorded balance is less than previously-sent amounts. (We implement a concrete admissible domain: sender sends a positive amount >= MinSum, waits past unlockTime, then Collect of that amount must succeed and the recorded balance must be >= amount in the correct contract; the mutant that did not increase balance will either allow Collect to withdraw despite low recorded balance or will behave inconsistently.)

For any caller and any nonzero ether amount A and unlockTime T, after calling Put(T) with value A the reference contract's recorded Acc[caller].balance increases by exactly A (so Acc[caller].balance >= A when previous balance was 0); the mutant that omits updating balance leaves balance unchanged and thus for some inputs (caller with initial 0 balance, A>0) this rule is violated.

After a successful Put that increases the contract's balance, a subsequent Collect (for an allowed amount) leaves the contract's locked_ mechanism such that a second Collect in a new call still succeeds (i.e., Collect does not permanently block further Collect calls), which is observable as the caller being able to receive funds twice in succession.

A single successful Collect call from an address must not permanently block subsequent Collect calls from the same address within new transactions (i.e., after one successful Collect, a later Collect with the same caller and valid conditions should still be allowed and not always revert).

If a call to Collect(...) succeeds (does not revert) then a subsequent call to Collect(...) with the same caller, same or smaller amount, and with unchanged time/conditions must also be allowed (i.e., not permanently blocked by reentrancy lock).

If the first Collect call from this test contract succeeds, then the second Collect call (with amount no greater than the first) must also succeed; i.e. firstReverted || (!secondReverted && am2 <= am1).

If the first Collect call from this test contract succeeds, then the second Collect call (with amount no greater than the first) must also succeed; i.e. firstReverted || (!secondReverted && am2 <= am1).

After a successful Collect(...) call by an account with sufficient balance and unlockTime passed, the reference contract allows future Collect(...) calls (modifier unlocks), whereas the mutant that never resets locked_ will cause subsequent Collect calls to always revert; thus: for any actor/amount/unlockTime that makes the first Collect succeed, the reference permits a second Collect (try-call returns true) while the mutant makes the second Collect revert (try-call returns false).

For any caller/amount/unlockTime where an initial Collect(...) call succeeds, the reference contract allows a subsequent Collect(...) call (modifier resets locked_), whereas the mutant that never unlocks will make that second Collect revert.

For any caller, amount and unlock time where an initial Collect succeeds, the correct contract allows a subsequent immediate Collect call (modifier releases lock) while the mutated contract that never resets the reentrancy lock causes that second Collect to revert.

For any account that has deposited at least MinSum and whose unlockTime has passed, the reference contract allows two sequential successful Collect(...) calls (both return true), whereas the mutant that never resets the reentrancy lock causes the second Collect(...) call to revert (return false) for some such inputs.

For any actor/amount/unlockTime where the actor has enough balance and unlockTime passed so that the first Collect succeeds, the reference contract allows a subsequent Collect call to NOT revert (modifier resets locked_), whereas the mutant that never resets locked_ causes the second Collect to revert for some inputs.
